name: @fossil-lang/corpus
description: Open a fossil corpus and read it. `open` is the door: it runs the fossil-graph verb surface as verb→SQL in WASM (fossil-graph-wasm) and delegates execution to a host-provided DuckDB-WASM query callback (e.g. keasy's Mosaic coordinator) — the larger-than-RAM query layer for whatever draws the graph; fossil ships no viewer. The addressing comes off the same WASM reader and is NOT a second import: `corpus.addressing` is the resolved plan the door already built, turning a GraphAr manifest into tile URLs by asking fossil-graph, which is the only implementation of it.
//name: This was `@fossil-lang/graph` and it does not draw one. Its door is `open`, what comes back is a `Corpus`, and every type it exports is `Corpus*` — the door spelled the word outright as `openCorpus` when this rename was argued, so the evidence for the package's name is now the type it answers with rather than the name that answers. The package that DOES put vertices on a GPU — `@kanzo-tech/graph` — is its one viewer, and two entries called `graph` in one `package.json` meant nothing about an import told you which. The Rust crates behind it are deliberately NOT renamed: `fossil-graph` is a verb surface over a property graph, which is what it says it is, and a cargo name is not in the import space this collision happened in. See /docs/design/corpus.
//exports: ONE entry, and there were four. `.` is the door and it exports THREE values plus the writer's role table: `open` and the two errors. **`resolveCorpus` came off it and did not come back under another name**: its answer is `corpus.addressing`, which every open resolves first, and `open` always takes an engine. `GRAPH_INFO_PATH` and `initFossilGraphWasm` stay off: the boot is awaited inside the door, and the index's file name is the door's business. Every part of this still needs the WASM — `corpus.js`, `client.js`, `load.js` and `address.js` all static-import `../pkg/fossil_graph_wasm.js`, so a consumer without that build output cannot load the barrel at all. `./corpus` went when the door reached the verbs. `./address` went when the addressing did: its whole justification was a closure that reached no WASM, and the only way to keep that promise was a second implementation of `crates/fossil-graph/src/plan.rs` in TypeScript. Composing a URL now costs loading a wasm module and an `await`, and that is the price of there being one reader behind one name.
//contract: `conformance/`, `guards/` and `integration/` are the corpus contract, and they live beside the reader that fulfils it rather than in a private app of their own: a private app beside a package is a second workspace name for one directory, and the package's own tests already reached into it by path. None of the three is in `files`, so npm never sees them. `guards/` stays plain ESM with no dependencies and no build — node plus the `duckdb` binary — because it is the directory a third party copies. **`test` is still `vitest run` over `tests/` and nothing else**, and that is the constraint this move must not break: `release.yml` runs `pnpm --filter "./packages/*" test` before publishing, and a suite that spawns `duckdb` in that step is what took `v0.3.0-alpha.4` down. The contract runs under its own names: `test:contract` is the guards' self-test and the conformance chain (`--without-wasm`, as `corpus.yml` runs it), `conformance` is every leg and FAILS without `pkg/`, and `test:integration` is the four suites that write a corpus with the `duckdb` binary and read it back through `src/`, under their own vitest config.

scripts.build: pnpm run build:wasm && pnpm run gen:types && tsc -p tsconfig.json
scripts.test:contract: node guards/self-test.mjs && node conformance/containers.mjs && node guards/check.mjs conformance/corpus && node conformance/provenance.mjs && node conformance/verify.mjs --without-wasm
